sentences.text: She should not have asked about the four hundred and six.
She knew it at the time.

The hare had said, very clearly, that it did not enjoy discussing them, and Marisol had heard that and had waited nearly a week, and then had asked anyway, because she was twelve and because a locked drawer is a locked drawer.
The hare did not refuse.

It went to the corner of the office where the oldest papers were — the ones gone soft and furred at the edges, held down with a flint instead of an acorn — and it pulled one out with its teeth and unrolled it across the slate with a paw at each corner.
"Nineteen forty-six," it said.
The map showed a stretch of country Marisol half recognised: the valley on the other side of the ridge, before the reservoir, when the reservoir was still a river and three farms.
And there was a path on it, drawn firmly, dashed, with a scale bar.
It went from a farm gate up over the shoulder of the hill to a chapel.
"That's a good path," said the hare.
"That is one of the best I ever did.
The gradient is right, it avoids the wet ground in February, it comes out at the chapel from the south so you get the light on the door.
A person walking that path would have enjoyed it every single time." "What happened?" "Nothing happened.
That is precisely the difficulty." It sat back.
"The first person did not go.
I had them — a woman at the farm, thirty-one, walked to the chapel on a Sunday and back, every week, and the road went round the long way and she resented it.
Everything was in place.
She had the reason and the temper and the legs." The hare's ears went flat and then came up again.
"And in the March her sister got ill in Tarragona, and she went down to nurse her, and she did not come back.
That is all.
There is no more to it than that." Marisol looked at the dashed line going up over the shoulder of the hill to the chapel with the light on the door.
"Couldn't somebody else have gone?" "Somebody else did not have her reason.
That is what people never understand about this." It turned the map round to look at it the right way up, which Marisol thought it probably did not need to do.
"A path is not a good idea.
A path is one person's bad afternoon, repeated by strangers who never knew about the afternoon.
If you take away the afternoon, there is nothing left to repeat." "So it's just — gone." "It is under a dozen metres of water now, along with the farm and the chapel.
But it was gone long before the reservoir.
It was gone in the March of nineteen forty-six." It rolled the map up.
"I keep them because somebody should.
That is the entire reason and I have stopped looking for a better one." Marisol sat back on her heels in the wet bracken.
"Doesn't that make you want to stop?" The hare put the flint back on the roll.
"Four hundred and six," it said.
"In two hundred and twelve years.
Which means the other ones are out there being walked on, right now, this minute, by people who think the ground has always been like that." It went back to the desk.
"You are standing in the light again." She moved.
She thought about that conversation for a long time afterwards, and the part she came back to was not the woman who went to Tarragona.
It was the arithmetic.
Two hundred and twelve years, and it had counted the failures precisely and had not, as far as she could tell, counted the others at all.
